steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The product life cycle has five stages: development (R&D, no sales), introduction (launch, low sales, high costs), growth (rapid sales increase, profits rise), maturity (sales peak then slow, high competition), decline (sales and profits fall).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Extension strategies try to extend the maturity stage: new features, new markets, rebranding, packaging changes, limited editions, or price promotions. They delay decline but don't prevent it permanently.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Product portfolio (or product mix) is the range of products a business sells: having products at different life cycle stages balances cash flow - mature products fund the development of new ones.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Product differentiation makes a product stand out from competitors: unique features, superior quality, distinctive branding, innovative design, or exceptional service.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe the four main stages of the product life cycle and explain what happens to sales and profit at each stage. | Explain two extension strategies a business could use to delay the decline of a product. | Evaluate whether a business should invest in extension strategies for a declining product or focus on developing new products.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Draw the product life cycle diagram in your answer - it shows AO1 knowledge and makes your explanation clearer. Extension strategies don't prevent decline - they only delay it. Use this in evaluation. Always link the product life cycle to cash flow: introduction = negative cash flow, maturity = positive cash flow.
